newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: INTERVIEW-Lion Nathan backs regional beers.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Lion Nathan backs regional beers.

text.p: Brewer Lion Nathan Ltd is set to make a virtue of its clutch of regional beer brands as it aims to claw back market share in Australia from the popular national brands of rival Foster's Brewing Group Ltd.

New Zealand-based Lion Nathan, which earlier on Monday reported a 21 percent fall in net earnings for the first half to February 28, has given itself six months to stabilise a long-term fall in Australian market share.

"Our objective was to put a floor under the decline (in market share) and we are very encouraged by some of the short-term results," said the chief executive of Lion's Australian brewing operations, Gordon Cairns.
Further out, the company will attempt to reclaim market share, which has fallen from around 50 percent in the late 1980s to about 40-41 percent at present.

Cairns declined to give details of the longer-term strategy, but said in a telephone interview he saw no need for Lion to try to match Foster's brewing arm Carlton & United Breweries and create a national brand in the mould of Victoria Bitter.
"Quite frankly I can't think why you would want to take Tooheys to Western Australia when they have a powerhouse of a brand there called Emu," he said.
"I can't think why you would want to take West End to Queensland when they've got a powerhouse of a brand there called Fourex," he added.
"It always struck me as commonsense to use what you've got."
Lion's brands include popular state-based beers such as Emu in Western Australia, Fourex in Queensland, West End in Adelaide and Tooheys in New South Wales.
"We think that's an enormous strength of ours, the fact that regionality, or parochialism, is important in the decision-making when you buy beer."

Cairns said he was heartened by recent signs of a pick-up in Australian market share, including a turnaround in the largest state of New South Wales, where the Tooheys brand has been in a long-term decline.
Lion's national market share rose from 40.6 percent for the three months to end-November 1996 to 40.9 percent in the three months to end-February 1997.
Market share for the month of March was 42 percent, although Cairns warned monthly figures were more volatile.
"While the results are encouraging I'd like us to give ourselves more time to ensure we have a stable platform," he said.
Lion has committed itself to stabilising brand share and earnings before interest and tax (EBIT) in its second half to end-August.
Cairns said Lion has reinvested in its brands -- the advertising and marketing outlay will double to A$30 million in the second half -- and has concentrated on regional brands.
"Instead of trying to be all things to all men, we are focusing on the big brands that are the main difference between us and our competitor," he said.
Lion has also distinguished between its products, selling some such as Tooheys Blue on price.
Others such as Tooheys New are "differentiated" from the rest of the market through advertising and promotional support and are sold at a premium.
"The differentiated brands are our major brands and get advertising support and the ones we are really banking the future of the company on," he said.
